overview: This record best fits the kingdom of Sind ruled by Dahir before the Arab conquest. Its broad outline includes neighboring frontier regions and should not be read as a precise border. The imported 700 to 800 interval crosses a major change: Dahir was defeated and killed in 712, and Arab provincial rule followed. It does not represent one Hindu kingdom surviving unchanged until 800.

periods.title: The Chach dynasty
periods.summary: A Brahman ruling family succeeded earlier kings; precise early reign dates remain debated.

periods.title: Conquest and resistance
periods.summary: Muhammad ibn Qasim defeated Dahir and extended caliphal power.

periods.title: Towns continue under new rulers

sections.title: A kingdom and the stories told about it

items.text: The later Chachnama preserves a tradition about earlier rulers at Aror and the rise of the Brahman Chach, whose family ruled before the conquest. Its account combines royal succession with questions of caste, loyalty and legitimacy. Historians must distinguish that remembered dynasty from every dramatic detail told about its members.

The surviving Persian Chachnama was produced in the thirteenth century, long after Dahir. Historian Manan Ahmed reads it as a work about political authority, legitimacy and the responsibilities of rulers, rather than a straightforward translation of an earlier conquest record. Other scholars allow more inherited material. Its stories require careful interpretation.

In the Chachnama’s story, Chach first succeeds as a scribe, and a queen helps him reach the throne. Advice, writing skills and family alliances matter alongside soldiers. These are themes of a later political narrative; they do not give us a school timetable or establish how every household lived.

Xuanzang describes wheat, millet, livestock and small, one-humped camels. He also reports differently colored salts used medicinally. His seventh-century account records historical remedies, not proof that they worked.

Banbhore stood beside the Gharo creek in the Indus delta region, where remains from several periods include a fortified center, harbor installations, workshops and urban quarters. Its position connected river-country communities to sea routes. Identifying it with the famous port of Debal is plausible but remains debated.

Excavations at Banbhore have produced glass, ivory and worked shells from both pre-Islamic and Islamic phases. Such materials preserve the work of people who shaped useful and decorative objects. The port’s history includes makers and customers, as well as rulers and visiting ships.

The Banbhore museum separates painted pottery dating before the conquest from eighth-century storage jars and white-paste pottery. These ordinary containers help show change across the political transition. A big jar is evidence of storage, but its original contents need separate evidence: an empty pot does not come with a surviving grocery label.

Researchers at Banbhore found clay moulds with repeated cells, nicknamed honeycomb moulds. They relate these to metalworking and coin production during the site’s long history. Studying an unfinished object or a workshop tool can reveal a manufacturing process that a finished treasure conceals.

A water tank discovered beneath later Banbhore buildings is tentatively linked to ninth-century urban changes. It belongs after Dahir’s kingdom, showing that residents continued investing in water infrastructure. The discovery cannot establish that seventh-century homes had the same system, still less private flushing toilets.

sections.title: Belief, small money and surviving writing

items.text: At Tharro, archaeologist N. G. Majumdar reported over a hundred small Buddhist tablets inside a mass of unbaked clay. Some showed a seated Buddha, others a row of shrines. Their inscriptions were assigned to the seventh or eighth century. These modest offerings show religious expression through clay and writing, beyond royal monuments.

A study of small silver pieces reportedly found near the Sindh-Baluchistan border examined 254 specimens. Most weighed about 1.15 to 1.25 grams, and their average diameter was around 16 millimeters. Their ruler and exact place of issue remain uncertain; dealer-reported findspots cannot substitute for a recorded excavation.

The same study reads one Brahmi inscription as ha-ma-va, a scholarly transliteration of three letter-units. Its meaning is unknown: it might be an abbreviation or control mark. Even the function of these unusual pieces has been debated. We can show the reading without inventing a translation or calling it Dahir’s motto.
Xuanzang calls Sind “信度國” (Xìndù guó), “country of Sind”. This seventh-century Chinese witness, shown in modern type and pinyin, records an outsider’s name rather than local speech.

sections.title: Conquest did not mean everyone disappeared

items.text: Al-Baladhuri’s ninth-century history describes both violent fighting and negotiated submission. At Alor, it reports an agreement to spare inhabitants and leave temples standing, while imposing tribute. This was a change of political power with different local outcomes, not one identical experience for every town.

ending.text: Dahir’s defeat and death in 712 ended his kingship. Conquest and resistance continued afterward, while towns and religious communities faced new rulers and tributary obligations. The atlas endpoint of 800 is a map cutoff, not the date when Sind’s people or culture vanished.
